title: ACWM-RM: A Reference-Free Reward Modelfrom Complementary Mismatch Preferences

paper.title: ACWM-RM: A Reference-Free Reward Model from Complementary Mismatch Preferences
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning has gained attention for improving action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), as it enables reward-driven optimization of visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF) beyond flow-matching optimization.
Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF.
However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ.
Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies.
In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos.
We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation.
To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos.
We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos.
Evaluation on AVM-Eval reveals the limited reliability of IDMs on generated videos, while downstream RL experiments show that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in both criteria.

sections.heading: 1 introduction
sections.text: Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2025 ) predict videos conditioned on robot actions, supporting embodied policy evaluation and optimization. For these applications, generated videos must preserve visual quality while faithfully reflecting the commanded actions. However, standard flow-matching training ( Lipman et al., 2022 ) does not explicitly optimize these criteria. This motivates reinforcement learning (RL) such as Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026a ) , which optimizes these criteria using rewards. The effectiveness of RL, however, depends on reward signals that reliably rank videos generated under the same conditioning input, assigning higher scores to those with better visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF). Existing reward signals fall into two main categories. First, full-reference rewards ( Wu et al., 2026b ) use metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS to compare generated videos with the corresponding ground-truth videos, providing VQ supervision but requiring reference videos and not directly assessing AF. Second, inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards ( Seo et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) assess AF without requiring reference videos by comparing actions inferred from generated videos with the input actions used to generate those videos, but do not directly assess VQ. Moreover, IDMs are typically trained on real-world videos, where motion and interactions obey physical laws, but are applied during RL to ACWM-generated videos that may contain visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies, such as robot-arm deformation and interpenetration. To quantify this issue, we generate 100 videos with each of four ACWMs under identical inputs. As shown in Figure , ACWM-generated videos exhibit more visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies than real-world videos. This gap raises the question of whether strong action-mismatch discrimination on real videos translates to reliable assessment of generated videos. In this work, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs. It evaluates how reliably IDMs assess AF on real videos using action-mismatch pairs and on generated videos using video-mismatch pairs. We then propose a reward model (ACWM-RM) for jointly assessing VQ and AF without ground-truth videos at reward computation time. To train ACWM-RM, we construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs of two types that provide complementary supervision: Action-mismatch pairs contrast original and perturbed actions for the same real video, providing AF supervision; Video-mismatch pairs contrast different generated videos under the same actions, providing VQ supervision while exposing the model to the generated-video distribution. For training strategy, we first pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on features extracted from real robot videos by a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) , establishing a dynamics representation for AF evaluation. We then jointly optimize the predictor and patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref, transferring the dynamics learned from real-world videos to AF assessment of generated videos. Our evaluation of four architecturally distinct IDMs on AVM-Eval shows that accurate AF assessment on real videos does not ensure reliable AF evaluation of generated videos. The best-performing IDM achieves 86.1% accuracy on action-mismatch pairs from real videos but only 70.0% on video-mismatch pairs from generated videos. To evaluate ACWM-RM’s downstream effectiveness as an RL reward, we fine-tune DreamDojo-2B with Flow-GRPO, comparing ACWM-RM against the best-performing IDM on AVM-Eval, a metric-based reward, and a VLM-based reward. On held-out tasks, ACWM-RM yields the best VQ and AF, while maintaining VLM-assessed physical consistency (PC) scores close to the original model before RL fine-tuning. Our main contributions: (1) We introduce AVM-Eval and show that, across four IDMs, accurate AF assessment on real videos does not ensure reliable AF evaluation of generated videos. (2) We develop AVM-Pref and ACWM-RM, combining dynamics pretraining with complementary mismatch preferences to assess both criteria without references during reward computation. (3) We demonstrate that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in VQ and AF when used for RL fine-tuning.

sections.heading: 2.1 Action-Conditioned World Models
sections.text: Action-conditioned world models generate videos conditioned on past observations and actions, simulating the resulting robot interactions to support policy evaluation and planning. To learn transferable dynamics, DreamDojo ( Gao et al., 2026 ) pretrains on human videos using continuous latent actions and adapts to target robots with robot data. To condition predictions on actions, iVideoGPT ( Wu et al., 2024 ) models observations and actions as token sequences with an autoregressive transformer, whereas IRASim ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) strengthens action-frame alignment through frame-level conditioning in a diffusion transformer. These predictive capabilities enable downstream applications: Genie Envisioner ( Liao et al., 2025 ) uses GE-Sim for action-conditioned simulation and closed-loop policy evaluation. Such applications require generated videos to preserve both VQ and AF, motivating our study of rewards that jointly assess these properties for ACWM post-training.

sections.heading: 2.2 Reward Modeling for World Models
sections.text: Reliable reward signals are essential for effective RL, as they determine which properties of videos are optimized. For general video generation, VideoReward ( Liu et al., 2026b ) learns human preferences over visual quality and alignment. For embodied world models based on instructions, ReWorld ( Peng et al., 2026 ) and RoboAlign-R1 ( Wu et al., 2026a ) assess video quality and instruction alignment without evaluating correspondence with numerical actions. For action-conditioned world models, RLVR-World ( Wu et al., 2026b ) provides visual rewards through ground-truth video comparisons, while RLIR ( Ye et al., 2025 ) provides AF rewards by using IDM. Other dynamics-based rewards target different properties: EVA ( Wang et al., 2026 ) assesses action executability using IDM. However, reference-based rewards require ground truth, and IDMs that are accurate on real videos does not ensure reliable evaluation of generated videos or joint assessment of VQ and AF.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: We first describe AVM-Eval construction (Sec. 4.1 ) and then our ACWM-RM, including AVM-Pref construction, model architecture, and two-stage training (Sec. 4.2 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark
sections.text: Existing IDMs are normally trained and evaluated on real-world videos. However, IDM-based rewards are applied to generated videos, whose distributions can differ from those of real-world videos. Generated videos may contain visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies, including robot-arm deformation and interpenetration, absent from real videos. To our knowledge, no existing benchmark compares the reliability of IDM-based AF assessment on real and generated videos. To address this gap, we construct AVM-Eval using a pairwise evaluation protocol ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) . AVM-Eval compares the reliability of AF assessment on real and ACWM-generated videos, using action-mismatch pairs and video-mismatch pairs , respectively. We next describe the source data preparation and benchmark construction.

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Source data preparation
sections.text: We use AgiBotWorld ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , a large-scale bimanual robot dataset with real-world videos, as one source dataset, and partition its data by task into three subsets: Agi A \mathrm{Agi_{A}} , Agi B \mathrm{Agi_{B}} , and Agi C \mathrm{Agi_{C}} . Covering 36 tasks, Agi A \mathrm{Agi_{A}} is split at the episode level into 34.0k training episodes ( Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} ) for IDM, ACWM-RM predictor pretraining, and AVM-Pref construction, and 2.2k testing episodes ( Agi A test \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{test}} ) for constructing seen-task evaluation pairs in AVM-Eval. Using Agi ​ _ ​ B \mathrm{Agi\_B} , which contains 10.0k episodes across 30 tasks, we construct pairs for both unseen-task evaluation in AVM-Eval and RL fine-tuning. To evaluate RL-optimized ACWMs, we use Agi C \mathrm{Agi_{C}} , which contains 1.5k episodes across 10 tasks. Additionally, to evaluate the embodiment and scene generalization of the IDMs in AVM-Eval, we use other bimanual robot datasets from Genie-Sim ( Gen \mathrm{Gen} ) ( Yin et al., 2026 ) , RoboDojo ( Robo D \mathrm{Robo_{D}} ) ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , and RoboTwin ( Robo T \mathrm{Robo_{T}} ) ( Mu et al., 2025 ) . sections.heading: 4.1.2 AVM-Eval Construction
sections.text: AVM-Eval comprises two complementary types of pairs: A video-mismatch pair holds the action chunk fixed and contrasts two videos, whereas an action-mismatch pair holds the video fixed and contrasts two action chunks. Together, these two types constitute 67.2k pairs in AVM-Eval. Action-mismatch pairs (53.9k). To evaluate IDM-based AF assessment on real videos, we construct action-mismatch pairs. Each pair is represented as ( I 0 , 𝐚 + , 𝐚 − , 𝐈 ) (I_{0},\mathbf{a}^{+},\mathbf{a}^{-},\mathbf{I}) , where 𝐚 + \mathbf{a}^{+} is the action chunk recorded with 𝐈 \mathbf{I} and 𝐚 − \mathbf{a}^{-} is a perturbed counterpart. We generate 𝐚 − \mathbf{a}^{-} using two types of perturbations: Numerical Perturbations (N-P) and Semantic Perturbations (S-P). N-P probe sensitivity to low-level numerical errors in end-effector translation and rotation magnitudes or directions, gripper opening degree, and action ordering. S-P probe sensitivity to high-level semantic errors through position offsets during grasping or placement, incorrect gripper timing, and mid-motion drift or freeze. We also perturb action chunks from Gen \mathrm{Gen} , Robo D \mathrm{Robo_{D}} , and Robo T \mathrm{Robo_{T}} to assess IDM generalization across embodiments and scenes. Detailed perturbation procedures are provided in Appendix A . Video-mismatch pairs (13.3k). To evaluate AF on generated videos, we considered constructing action-mismatch pairs in the same way. However, ACWMs cannot guarantee that generated videos faithfully follow the action chunk, so a perturbed action chunk may be more consistent with the generated video than the original action chunk, reversing the intended preference label. We therefore construct video-mismatch pairs by fixing the action chunk and ranking generated videos using WorldArena’s nDTW ( Shang et al., 2026 ) for AF, with additional filtering to limit the influence of visual quality (Appendix B ). We use four ACWMs with varying AF performance: DreamDojo-2B (DD-2B), DreamDojo-14B (DD-14B) ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , GE-Sim-2B (GE-2B), and OSCAR-2B (OS-2B) ( Wu and Gao, 2026 ) . Under the same I 0 I_{0} and 𝐚 \mathbf{a} , each ACWM independently samples six 12-frame videos using the stochastic SDE sampler adopted by Flow-GRPO. Within each ACWM, we pair a higher-nDTW video 𝐈 ^ + \hat{\mathbf{I}}^{+} with a lower-nDTW video 𝐈 ^ − \hat{\mathbf{I}}^{-} to form an intra-model pair ( I 0 , 𝐚 , 𝐈 ^ + , 𝐈 ^ − ) (I_{0},\mathbf{a},\hat{\mathbf{I}}^{+},\hat{\mathbf{I}}^{-}) . We rank videos generated by any two ACWMs under the same input to construct cross-model pairs .

sections.heading: 4.2 Reward Model for Action-Conditioned World Models

Existing rewards provide only partial supervision, with metric-based rewards also requiring ground-truth videos. We therefore propose ACWM-RM, a reference-free reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF. We next describe the construction of its training dataset, termed AVM-Pref (Sec. 4.2.1 ), followed by the architecture and the two-stage training strategy (Sec. 4.2.2 ).

sections.heading: 4.2.1 AVM-Pref Construction
sections.text: To train ACWM-RM with the Bradley-Terry loss, we construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) from Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} , comprising 506.3k action-mismatch and video-mismatch pairs that provide complementary supervision. Action-mismatch pairs (156.3k) : We use the same numerical and semantic action perturbations as AVM-Eval to provide AF supervision. Video-mismatch pairs (350k) : We follow AVM-Eval to generate videos from four ACWMs and construct intra-model and cross-model pairs, but use four visual quality metrics (global and local PSNR and LPIPS) instead of nDTW to provide VQ supervision. Since action-mismatch pairs already provide broader AF supervision than nDTW’s 2D trajectory alignment, including translation, rotation, and gripper opening, we use video-mismatch pairs for complementary VQ supervision. Although action-mismatch pairs use real videos and thus differ from the generated-video distribution, our empirical results show that combining both types improves AF assessment on generated videos. Finally, to reduce sampling bias, we aim for comparable pair counts across models and tasks for intra-model pairs and across model combinations and tasks for cross-model pairs. Appendix C details how the four metrics are used, while Appendix H provides AVM-Pref statistics.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 Reward Model Architecture and Training Strategy
sections.text: ACWM-RM scores a candidate video conditioned on an action chunk and its associated state sequence, producing a scalar reward for VQ and AF. It consists of a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder E E , a bimanual action-conditioned predictor P ϕ P_{\phi} , and a patch-weighted score head h ψ h_{\psi} . Training proceeds in two stages: dynamics pretraining optimizes P ϕ P_{\phi} on real-world videos, while preference training jointly optimizes P ϕ P_{\phi} and h ψ h_{\psi} on AVM-Pref to adapt the learned dynamics for AF assessment. Dynamics pretraining. Following V-JEPA 2-AC ( Assran et al., 2025 ) , we pretrain P ϕ P_{\phi} with E E frozen. Unlike the original single-arm setting, our predictor takes bimanual actions. For bimanual inputs, we express actions and states in a coordinate system aligned with the head-camera axes, normalize them, project them to the predictor’s hidden dimension, and add a learnable identity embedding for each arm. sections.heading: 5 experiments
sections.text: We first describe experimental setup (Sec. 5.1 ) and evaluate IDMs and ACWM-RM on AVM-Eval (Sec. 5.2 ). We then compare Flow-GRPO reward signals (Sec. 5.3 ) and conduct ablations (Sec. 5.4 ).

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Baselines. On AVM-Eval, we compare ACWM-RM with four architecturally distinct IDMs: EVA-IDM ( EVA I \mathrm{EVA_{I}} ) ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , which uses a convolutional backbone; GR00T-IDM ( GRT I \mathrm{GRT_{I}} ) ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , which uses a diffusion-based model; TAP-IDM ( TAP I \mathrm{TAP_{I}} ) ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , a vision-language model equipped with an action expert; and J-IDM ( J I \mathrm{J_{I}} ) ( Li et al., 2026 ) , which recovers actions by inverting a predicted per-pixel Jacobian field. This evaluates how reliably IDMs with different architectures transfer from real-video training to generated-video evaluation. For Flow-GRPO training of ACWMs, we compare ACWM-RM with IDM-based, metric-based, and VLM-based rewards. The IDM-based baseline uses the best-performing IDM on AVM-Eval. The metric-based baseline combines the four visual quality metrics used in AVM-Pref following the fusion procedure of RLVR-World ( Wu et al., 2026b ) . We further explore whether VLM-as-a-Judge ( Hong et al., 2025 ) can provide effective rewards for ACWM optimization. Specifically, we use Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct to score videos using embodiment-specific prompts and criteria from RBench. Prompts and criteria definitions are provided in the Appendix F . Training setup. We train the four IDMs on Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} using their official pretrained backbones and implementations, following the original training paradigm of predicting actions from real-world videos. Each IDM and ACWM-RM has a nominal budget of approximately 7.12M 13-frame video draws, including both ACWM-RM training stages. For Flow-GRPO, we fine-tune DreamDojo-2B on Agi B \mathrm{Agi_{B}} and evaluate it on Agi C \mathrm{Agi_{C}} . Implementation details for the IDMs, ACWM-RM, and Flow-GRPO are provided in Appendices E , D , and G , respectively. Evaluation protocol. We evaluate IDMs using pairwise accuracy on AVM-Eval. For each ACWM optimized with Flow-GRPO, we repeat video generation five times and report the mean and standard deviation of the following metrics across runs: (1) VQ, measured by PSNR, LPIPS, SSIM, MSE, and FVD; (2) AF, measured by nDTW, a proxy based on the alignment of generated and ground-truth 2D manipulator trajectories; and (3) physical consistency, assessed by GPT-5.6 sol using the same prompt and criteria as the VLM-based reward, covering Object Consistency (OC), Manipulator Consistency (MC), and Anomaly Check (AC). sections.heading: 5.3 Flow-GRPO with Different Reward Signals
sections.text: We evaluate ACWMs trained with different rewards on Agi C \mathrm{Agi_{C}} along the following dimensions. Visual quality. ACWM-RM achieves the best results across all five VQ metrics in Table 5 , outperforming the full-reference metric-based reward. Unlike this baseline, ACWM-RM requires no ground-truth videos for reward computation during RL. Although its training preferences are derived from PSNR and LPIPS, the gains extend to SSIM, MSE, and FVD, which are not used for preference supervision. In contrast, the IDM-based reward degrades all five metrics relative to Origin, suggesting that optimizing IDM-based AF alone is insufficient to preserve visual quality. Action-following fidelity. Table 4 shows that ACWM-RM is the only evaluated reward that improves nDTW over Origin, from 14.84 to 16.41. The VLM-based and metric-based rewards yield no improvement, while the IDM-based reward reduces nDTW to 13.21 despite explicitly measuring consistency between inferred and conditioning actions. Together with the AVM-Eval findings, these results suggest that strong action-mismatch discrimination on real videos does not necessarily translate into an effective RL reward for improving action-following fidelity. Physical consistency. Although ACWM-RM does not explicitly reward physical consistency, the model optimized with it achieves scores comparable to Origin across all three criteria in Table 5 . By contrast, the VLM-based reward yields a lower overall physical-consistency score than Origin (3.86 vs. 4.00), despite directly targeting these criteria. One possible explanation is disagreement between the VLMs used for reward computation and evaluation: optimizing scores assigned by the reward VLM may not improve physical consistency as judged by the evaluation VLM.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work
sections.text: Through AVM-Eval, we showed that strong action-mismatch discrimination on real videos does not ensure reliable AF assessment of generated videos. To address this limitation while also assessing VQ, we introduced ACWM-RM, a reward model requiring no ground-truth videos for reward computation. ACWM-RM outperforms IDMs on generated-video AF and, when used to fine-tune DreamDojo-2B, yields better VQ and AF than alternative reward signals. Limitations and future work. ACWM-RM is trained to assess VQ and AF, but does not explicitly supervise physical consistency (PC). Although RL fine-tuning with ACWM-RM maintains PC scores close to those of the pre-RL model, the reward does not directly target physical violations such as interpenetration. Moreover, downstream RL improvements have so far been demonstrated only for DreamDojo-2B on AgiBotWorld. Future work will incorporate physical-consistency supervision and evaluate ACWM-RM for RL optimization across a broader range of ACWMs.

sections.heading: A.1 Active Channel Identification
sections.text: ACWMs predict a stationary arm well but a moving arm poorly, so their prediction error is concentrated in the channels in which an arm is moving. These are therefore the channels a reward model has to discriminate, and we restrict perturbations to them. To identify these channels, we compute six Boolean activity flags, one per channel. Each flag is set from the spread of the absolute trajectory over the 13 frames rather than summed per-step absolute changes, preventing small mean-reverting servo jitter from being mistaken for sustained motion. The red dashed line marks the threshold calibrated for that channel, placed slightly to the right of the valley separating them. sections.heading: A.2 Numerical Action Perturbations
sections.text: Numerical action perturbations modify 𝐚 + \mathbf{a}^{+} using operators drawn from a perturbation pool whose membership is determined by the six activity flags. We first select the temporal windows within the action chunk to be edited, then assemble the perturbation pool, then apply the drawn perturbations channel by channel, and finally check whether the negative differs sufficiently from the positive.

sections.heading: Temporal Window Sampling.
sections.text: Perturbing every action would make the negative wrong everywhere, which is both easy to detect and unrepresentative of the localized errors an ACWM actually makes. We therefore confine each edit to a few windows of consecutive actions and leave the remaining actions clean. In addition, many different combinations of windows and perturbation operators remain available, so a single action chunk can yield many distinct negatives. The windows themselves are sampled in one of two ways. With probability 0.3, the whole chunk is taken as a single window. Retaining these fully perturbed negatives keeps a coarse difficulty level in the mix. Otherwise, we sample one to three windows, each covering one to seven consecutive actions, and require neighboring windows to be separated by at least one unedited action so that the edited segments stay distinguishable. If the sampled windows cannot all be placed within the 12 actions under this constraint, we drop windows until the remaining ones fit. In either case, the outcome is a set of windows 𝒲 = { [ w k lo , w k hi ] } \mathcal{W}=\{[w_{k}^{\rm lo},w_{k}^{\rm hi}]\} marking the actions to be edited, where k k indexes the windows and w k lo w_{k}^{\rm lo} , w k hi w_{k}^{\rm hi} are the first and last actions of window k k . The actions outside them stay clean.

sections.heading: Perturbation Pool Construction and Sampling.
sections.text: To enlarge the range of perturbation types, we build a perturbation pool for each action chunk to be perturbed. For every arm with an active translation flag, we draw one translation perturbation with equal probability from Magnitude , Direction , and Magnitude & Direction , and add it to the pool. For every arm with an active rotation flag, we draw one rotation perturbation with equal probability from Orientation Direction , Orientation Magnitude , and Orientation Magnitude & Direction , and add it to the pool. For every active gripper flag, we add one Gripper Perturbation operator to the pool. The pool further holds a global Gaussian Perturbation whenever at least one channel is active, together with a global Temporal Order Permutation operator. Each perturbation in the pool is then selected independently with probability 0.5, and if no perturbation is selected, we select one uniformly from the pool, so that every negative carries at least one edit. We initialize 𝐚 − = 𝐚 + \mathbf{a}^{-}=\mathbf{a}^{+} before applying the selected perturbations sequentially. All selected perturbations are applied one after another to all sampled windows to produce a single 𝐚 − \mathbf{a}^{-} , with the structured perturbations writing their own action dimensions, Gaussian noise added on top, and order permutation applied last.

sections.heading: A.3 Semantic Action Perturbations
sections.text: Semantic action perturbations differ from numerical action perturbations in what they edit and where the edits are applied. The semantic procedure never perturbs 𝐚 + \mathbf{a}^{+} directly, but edits the absolute state sequence 𝐬 \mathbf{s} and obtains 𝐚 − \mathbf{a}^{-} by differencing the edited states through Eq. 7 . The perturbation is anchored at a grasp, release, or mid-motion event rather than at an individual action, so the error corresponds to a semantic-level mistake. These events can be identified from the gripper events: a gripper closing marks a grasp, a gripper opening marks a release, and the interval between a closing and the following opening marks mid-motion drift or freeze. We therefore locate these events and anchor the semantic perturbations to them. Applying perturbation at a gripper event requires more context than a single clip provides. We therefore subsample the episode to 8 fps, detect the events and apply the perturbation over this whole subsampled episode, and crop the 13-frame clip afterward.

sections.heading: Gripper Event Detection.
sections.text: We first describe how gripper closing and opening events are extracted from an episode. Let γ max r \gamma_{\max}^{r} and γ min r \gamma_{\min}^{r} be the largest and smallest values it takes over the whole episode, γ t r \gamma_{t}^{r} be the gripper opening of arm r r , and ρ r = γ max r − γ min r \rho^{r}=\gamma_{\max}^{r}-\gamma_{\min}^{r} be its range. If ρ r < 5 \rho^{r}<5 degrees, the gripper never opens or closes appreciably. Otherwise set γ lo r = γ min r + 0.30 ​ ρ r , γ hi r = γ min r + 0.70 ​ ρ r . \gamma_{\rm lo}^{r}=\gamma_{\min}^{r}+0.30\rho^{r},\qquad\gamma_{\rm hi}^{r}=\gamma_{\min}^{r}+0.70\rho^{r}. (20) Here γ lo r \gamma_{\rm lo}^{r} and γ hi r \gamma_{\rm hi}^{r} are the closing and opening thresholds for arm r r , placed at 30% and 70% of that arm’s observed gripper range, so that the band between them spans the middle 40%. A single pass over the episode gives every frame an open or closed flag. Specifically, a frame is labeled close when its γ r \gamma^{r} falls below γ lo r \gamma_{\rm lo}^{r} and open when it rises above γ hi r \gamma_{\rm hi}^{r} , while frames lying between the two thresholds are left unlabeled. Whenever two consecutive labeled frames carry opposite labels, the interval between them is marked as an event, which is a gripper close event when the labels run from open to close and a gripper open event in the reverse case. Because the thresholds are 40% apart, fluctuations near one of them cannot produce an event. Then, for the mid-motion events, we scan each arm’s γ r \gamma^{r} over the episode and mark a maximal interval as mid-motion if γ r \gamma^{r} stays below γ lo r \gamma_{\rm lo}^{r} throughout while the end-effector displacement across the interval exceeds τ trans r \tau_{\mathrm{trans}}^{r} . (Intervals shorter than 25 frames are discarded.) Finally, the detected three events are used by the three semantic perturbations described below.

The first condition ensures that the crop overlaps the edited part of the episode, while the actions outside it stay clean and serve as context. sections.heading: B.1 nDTW-Based Pair Filtering
sections.text: We compute nDTW scores using the official implementation of WorldArena ( Shang et al., 2026 ) and filter candidate video pairs with small score differences. The threshold statistics are collected from rollouts conditioned on 240 input clips selected from Agi A test \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{test}} and Agi B \mathrm{Agi_{B}} , covering 30 tasks and 120 episodes, with eight clips per task. For each clip, DreamDojo-14B, DreamDojo-2B, GE-Sim-2B, and OSCAR-2B each generate six videos under the same initial frame and action chunk, giving 240 × 4 × 6 = 5,760 240\times 4\times 6=5{,}760 rollouts. For each input clip, we enumerate all ( 6 2 ) = 15 \binom{6}{2}=15 pairs within each model and all 6 × 6 = 36 6\times 6=36 pairs for each of the ( 4 2 ) = 6 \binom{4}{2}=6 model combinations. This gives 14,400 intra-model and 51,840 cross-model candidate pairs for the threshold statistics. Let s i s_{i} and s j s_{j} denote the nDTW scores ( × 100 \times 100 ) of two candidate videos relative to the same ground-truth video. We compute their absolute score difference as Δ i ​ j = | s i − s j | . \Delta_{ij}=|s_{i}-s_{j}|. (25) We pool these differences across input clips separately for intra-model and cross-model pairs, and set each filtering threshold to the 5th percentile of its corresponding distribution. As shown in Figure 4 , the resulting thresholds are τ intra = 0.03 \tau_{\mathrm{intra}}=0.03 and τ cross = 0.12 \tau_{\mathrm{cross}}=0.12 . We retain an intra-model pair only when Δ i ​ j ≥ τ intra \Delta_{ij}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{intra}} and a cross-model pair only when Δ i ​ j ≥ τ cross \Delta_{ij}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{cross}} , assigning the video with the higher score as preferred. This empirical filtering rule excludes approximately the lowest 5% of pairwise score differences in each distribution, removing candidate pairs with similar nDTW scores.

sections.heading: B.2 Visual Quality Control
sections.text: To limit the influence of visual quality on AF evaluation, we further filter the pairs retained above using global and local PSNR and LPIPS, computed against the shared ground-truth video (Appendix C ). To calibrate the thresholds, we construct candidate pairs from AgiBotWorld and order each pair by the quality metric being considered. For each metric m m and pair type c c (intra-model or cross-model), we set τ m , c \tau_{m,c} to the 2nd percentile of the resulting positive quality gaps (Figure 5 ). For the pairs retained by nDTW filtering, we keep their preference labels fixed and define the signed quality gap δ m \delta_{m} as positive-minus-negative for PSNR and negative-minus-positive for LPIPS. We retain a pair only if | δ m | ≤ τ m , c |\delta_{m}|\leq\tau_{m,c} for all four metrics. This ensures that the higher-nDTW and lower-nDTW videos have comparable visual quality within the empirical tolerances.

sections.text: This appendix details the four visual quality metrics and pair selection procedure used to construct video-mismatch pairs for AVM-Pref. A clip consists of a ground-truth (GT) video 𝐈 = ( I 0 , … , I K ) \mathbf{I}=(I_{0},\ldots,I_{K}) and a generated video 𝐈 ^ = ( I ^ 0 , … , I ^ K ) \hat{\mathbf{I}}=(\hat{I}_{0},\ldots,\hat{I}_{K}) , each with one initial frame and K K future frames. The initial frame serves as the conditioning input to the ACWM and is therefore shared, I ^ 0 = I 0 \hat{I}_{0}=I_{0} . The two global metrics assign one value to each future frame t = 1 , … , K t=1,\ldots,K and average these values over the clip. The two local metrics assign one value to each valid transition t : I t − 1 → I t t:I_{t-1}\!\rightarrow I_{t} , using the optical flow between the two frames to determine the regions to score; these values are then averaged over the valid transitions of the clip. The four metrics comprise two global metrics that evaluate the entire frame—global PSNR PSNR glob \mathrm{PSNR}^{\mathrm{glob}} (higher is better) and global LPIPS LPIPS glob \mathrm{LPIPS}^{\mathrm{glob}} (lower is better)—and two local metrics that evaluate only the regions containing motion—local PSNR PSNR loc \mathrm{PSNR}^{\mathrm{loc}} (higher is better) and local LPIPS LPIPS loc \mathrm{LPIPS}^{\mathrm{loc}} (lower is better).

sections.heading: C.1 Global Visual Quality Metrics
sections.text: Both global metrics compare each generated frame with the corresponding GT frame and average over all K K future frames. Unlike the local metrics below, they have a value on every future frame, so the average always runs over the full set { 1 , … , K } \{1,\ldots,K\} .

sections.text: For frame t t , MSE is computed over all pixels and RGB channels: MSE t = 1 3 ​ H ​ W ​ ∑ k = 1 3 ∑ i = 1 H ∑ j = 1 W ( I t ​ [ k , i , j ] − I ^ t ​ [ k , i , j ] ) 2 , PSNR t glob = 10 ​ log 10 ​ 255 2 MSE t , \mathrm{MSE}_{t}=\frac{1}{3HW}\sum_{k=1}^{3}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\sum_{j=1}^{W}\bigl(I_{t}[k,i,j]-\hat{I}_{t}[k,i,j]\bigr)^{2},\qquad\mathrm{PSNR}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{t}=10\log_{10}\frac{255^{2}}{\mathrm{MSE}_{t}}, (26) with the convention PSNR t glob = 99 \mathrm{PSNR}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{t}=99 whenever MSE t ≤ 10 − 12 \mathrm{MSE}_{t}\leq 10^{-12} , so that an exactly reproduced frame yields a finite score. The global PSNR of the clip is PSNR glob = 1 K ​ ∑ t = 1 K PSNR t glob . \mathrm{PSNR}^{\mathrm{glob}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{t=1}^{K}\mathrm{PSNR}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{t}. (27)

sections.heading: Global LPIPS.
sections.text: We use the official LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) implementation with the AlexNet backbone, loaded from a fixed local checkpoint so that every clip in the dataset is scored by identical weights. Frames are converted to RGB, scaled to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , and then affinely mapped once onto the network input range [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . Writing d LPIPS d_{\mathrm{LPIPS}} for the distance this network produces, the global LPIPS of the clip is LPIPS glob = 1 K ​ ∑ t = 1 K d LPIPS ​ ( I ^ t , I t ) . \mathrm{LPIPS}^{\mathrm{glob}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{t=1}^{K}d_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}\bigl(\hat{I}_{t},\,I_{t}\bigr). (28)

sections.heading: C.2 Motion Region Extraction
sections.text: Action-induced changes are confined to the local regions where the robot interacts with objects, and these are also the regions an ACWM is most likely to render incorrectly. Because the two global metrics average over the whole frame, the surrounding static background dilutes this evidence, making them less sensitive to the failures that matter most. The two local metrics therefore restrict their evaluation to these local regions. These regions are located from optical flow, estimated independently on the GT and on the generated video, so that the local metrics penalize both motion the ACWM fails to reproduce and motion it invents.

sections.heading: Optical Flow.
sections.text: We estimate optical flow with MegaFlow ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . For each video, we run the estimator on every pair of adjacent frames, obtaining fields: Φ t = MegaFlow ( I t − 1 , I t ) ∈ ℝ 2 × H × W , Φ ^ t = MegaFlow ( I ^ t − 1 , I ^ t ) , t = 1 , … , K . \Phi_{t}=\mathrm{MegaFlow}(I_{t-1},I_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times H\times W},\qquad\widehat{\Phi}_{t}=\mathrm{MegaFlow}(\hat{I}_{t-1},\hat{I}_{t}),\qquad t=1,\ldots,K. (29)

It is defined on the grid of frame t − 1 t-1 , where each vector Φ t [ : , i , j ] \Phi_{t}[:,i,j] gives the displacement of pixel ( i , j ) (i,j) between the two frames. We identify moving pixels by thresholding the displacement magnitude at τ = 2 \tau=2 pixels: S t = { ( i , j ) : ∥ Φ t [ : , i , j ] ∥ 2 > τ } . S_{t}=\bigl\{(i,j):\;\lVert\Phi_{t}[:,i,j]\rVert_{2}>\tau\bigr\}. (30) Thus, S t S_{t} contains the source positions of moving pixels in frame t − 1 t-1 . Their corresponding destination positions in frame t t are S t → = { ( clip ⁡ ( i + ⌊ Φ t v ​ [ i , j ] ⌉ ) , clip ⁡ ( j + ⌊ Φ t u ​ [ i , j ] ⌉ ) ) : ( i , j ) ∈ S t } , S^{\rightarrow}_{t}=\Bigl\{\bigl(\mathrm{clip}(i+\lfloor\Phi^{\mathrm{v}}_{t}[i,j]\rceil),\,\mathrm{clip}(j+\lfloor\Phi^{\mathrm{u}}_{t}[i,j]\rceil)\bigr):\;(i,j)\in S_{t}\Bigr\}, (31) where Φ t u \Phi^{\mathrm{u}}_{t} and Φ t v \Phi^{\mathrm{v}}_{t} denote the horizontal and vertical components of the optical flow at time t t , respectively. Here, ⌊ ⋅ ⌉ \lfloor\cdot\rceil denotes rounding to the nearest integer, and clip \mathrm{clip} restricts each coordinate to the valid range of the corresponding image axis. Using the same construction, we obtain the pixel sets S ^ t \widehat{S}_{t} and S ^ t → \widehat{S}^{\rightarrow}_{t} for the generated video from its optical flow field Φ ^ t \widehat{\Phi}_{t} . Since the resulting pixel sets may contain isolated or spatially scattered pixels, we group neighboring pixels into rectangular regions so that each local score corresponds to a coherent moving structure. Specifically, for a pixel set S S , let Box ⁡ ( S ) \mathrm{Box}(S) denote the collection of bounding boxes of its connected components, with one box assigned to each component. We discard any box whose area is smaller than 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} of the total frame area. The boxes extracted from the GT and generated videos are then merged frame by frame: ℬ t = Box ⁡ ( S t ) ∪ Box ⁡ ( S ^ t ) , ℬ t → = Box ⁡ ( S t → ) ∪ Box ⁡ ( S ^ t → ) , \mathcal{B}_{t}=\mathrm{Box}(S_{t})\cup\mathrm{Box}(\widehat{S}_{t}),\qquad\mathcal{B}^{\rightarrow}_{t}=\mathrm{Box}(S^{\rightarrow}_{t})\cup\mathrm{Box}(\widehat{S}^{\rightarrow}_{t}), (32) where ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} is defined on frame t − 1 t-1 and ℬ t → \mathcal{B}^{\rightarrow}_{t} on frame t t . sections.heading: Scored Regions.
sections.text: For each transition t t , we evaluate only the bounding boxes constructed above. The boxes in ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} are evaluated on the source frame t − 1 t-1 , and those in ℬ t → \mathcal{B}^{\rightarrow}_{t} on the destination frame t t . The box-level evaluations can be recorded as 𝒫 t = { ( b , t − 1 ) : b ∈ ℬ t } ∪ { ( b , t ) : b ∈ ℬ t → } , \mathcal{P}_{t}=\bigl\{(b,t-1):b\in\mathcal{B}_{t}\bigr\}\cup\bigl\{(b,t):b\in\mathcal{B}^{\rightarrow}_{t}\bigr\}, (33) where each pair specifies one box and the frame on which it is evaluated. For each metric, we first aggregate the box-level values within ℬ t \mathcal{B}_{t} and within ℬ t → \mathcal{B}^{\rightarrow}_{t} separately, and then aggregate these two set-level values into the score of transition t t . For each transition, we compute local metrics over the available bounding boxes, omitting any empty box set from aggregation. For t = 1 t=1 , the shared initial frame is excluded from local scoring, so only boxes in ℬ 1 → \mathcal{B}^{\rightarrow}_{1} contribute. We determine the valid transition set 𝒯 valid \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{valid}} separately for each GT-generated video comparison, skipping t t if neither video provides a valid scored box and discarding the clip only if this set is empty. Thus, a transition with no valid motion region in either video is omitted, whereas spurious motion in the generated video is still evaluated even when the GT is stationary.

sections.heading: C.4 Pair Selection
sections.text: A pair is retained only if the positive video strictly beats the negative one on all four metrics: higher global and local PSNR and lower global and local LPIPS. Pairs that do not satisfy all four inequalities are discarded. We aim for comparable pair counts across models and tasks for intra-model pairs, and across model combinations and tasks for cross-model pairs; the resulting distributions are reported in Appendix H , as shown in Figure 8 .

sections.text: For dynamics pretraining, preference training, and IDM training, we hold out internal validation subsets from Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} for checkpoint selection and exclude them from parameter optimization. sections.heading: D.1 Dynamics Pretraining
sections.text: This appendix specifies the input processing, predictor architecture, and dynamics-pretraining setup. The input processing and predictor architecture are shared by both training stages.

sections.heading: Input Representation.
sections.text: We use 13-frame clips sampled at 8 fps, with one initial frame and K = 12 K=12 future frames. Let 𝐈 = ( I 0 , … , I K ) \mathbf{I}=(I_{0},\ldots,I_{K}) denote a clip and 𝐚 = ( a 1 , … , a K ) \mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{K}) its associated action chunk, which consists of relative end-effector actions for both arms. The action a t a_{t} corresponds to the transition from frame I t − 1 I_{t-1} to frame I t I_{t} . Let 𝐬 = ( s 0 , … , s K − 1 ) \mathbf{s}=(s_{0},\ldots,s_{K-1}) denote the corresponding state sequence, where s t s_{t} records the end-effector states of both arms at frame I t I_{t} . For each arm r ∈ { L , R } r\in\{L,R\} , a t r ∈ ℝ 7 a_{t}^{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{7} comprises a 3D translation increment, a 3D rotation-vector increment, and a gripper-opening increment. The absolute end-effector state s t r ∈ ℝ 10 s_{t}^{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{10} comprises a 3D position, a continuous 6D rotation representation, and the gripper state. For predictor input, we group components by arm and write a t = ( a t L , a t R ) a_{t}=(a_{t}^{L},a_{t}^{R}) and s t = ( s t L , s t R ) s_{t}=(s_{t}^{L},s_{t}^{R}) . This arm-wise action layout differs from Eq. 6 , which groups the two arms’ translations, rotations, and gripper increments by component type. The two action layouts are related by a fixed permutation of components; this permutation changes their arrangement, not their values. The coordinate transformations and normalization used for predictor input are described below. We first transform the absolute end-effector position and orientation components of each arm’s state into the head-camera coordinate frame. For each arm, let p t p_{t} and Q t ∈ SO ⁡ ( 3 ) Q_{t}\in\mathrm{SO}(3) denote the transformed position and orientation. The state stores p t p_{t} and the first two columns of Q t Q_{t} as its position and 6D orientation representation, respectively. We then compute the translation and rotation components of the action from consecutive transformed states. Translation increments are Δ ​ p t = p t − p t − 1 \Delta p_{t}=p_{t}-p_{t-1} . Rotation increments use left composition, Δ ​ Q t = Q t ​ Q t − 1 ⊤ \Delta Q_{t}=Q_{t}Q_{t-1}^{\top} , and are encoded as rotation vectors ω t \omega_{t} in radians. For the gripper, we normalize the opening w t w_{t} as g t = clip ⁡ ( w t / 100 , 0 , 1 ) g_{t}=\operatorname{clip}(w_{t}/100,0,1) . The state stores the absolute normalized opening g t g_{t} , while the action stores its increment Δ ​ g t = g t − g t − 1 \Delta g_{t}=g_{t}-g_{t-1} . We then normalize the robot inputs by scaling the translation components of both arms’ actions by 65.48 65.48 and the rotation-vector components by 11.80 11.80 , leaving the gripper command unchanged. These coefficients are the reciprocals of the median per-step translation magnitude ( 0.015271 0.015271 m) and rotation magnitude ( 0.084724 0.084724 rad) computed from the training trajectories. This scaling brings the median magnitudes of both types of action increments to approximately one. We apply the same translation scaling factor of 65.48 65.48 to the XYZ components of the absolute states, since state positions and action translation increments are expressed in the same head-camera coordinate frame and share the same physical units (meters). The states’ 6D orientation representations consist of two orthonormal columns of a rotation matrix, whose dimensionless entries lie in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . These representations already have a fixed scale, so we retain them without additional scaling. Gripper states are already normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , and their increments lie in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , so neither needs rescaling. Each full frame is resized to 384 × 384 384\times 384 using bilinear interpolation, without cropping. We encode frames independently with the frozen V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-G/16 encoder, which has 48 layers, hidden dimension D = 1664 D=1664 , and approximately 1.84B parameters. With a patch size of 16 × 16 16\times 16 , each frame produces N = 24 × 24 = 576 N=24\times 24=576 tokens of dimension D D . sections.heading: Predictor Architecture.
sections.text: The predictor has 24 Transformer layers, hidden dimension d P = 1024 d_{P}=1024 , 16 attention heads per layer, and approximately 0.31B parameters. Block-causal attention lets a time block access itself and earlier blocks, but no future-frame blocks. Visual patches can therefore attend to both arms’ controls and the preceding visual history. After the Transformer blocks, conditioning tokens are discarded and predicted visual tokens are projected to dimension D = 1664 D=1664 for comparison with the encoder features.

sections.heading: Training Setup.
sections.text: We train for 120 epochs, sampling one clip per episode in each epoch, with a global batch of 256 clips (16 per GPU on 16 GPUs). Based on the reported 34k episodes, this corresponds to approximately 4.08M clip draws and 15.94k optimizer steps. The learning rate warms up from 7.5 × 10 − 5 7.5\times 10^{-5} to 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} over the first 10 % 10\% of training steps, remains constant for the next 45 % 45\% , and decays linearly to 10 − 6 10^{-6} over the final 45 % 45\% . sections.text: We initialize P ϕ P_{\phi} from dynamics pretraining and randomly initialize h ψ h_{\psi} , keeping E E frozen. The clip length, input representation, and predictor architecture follow Appendix D.1 . We expand on Sec. 4.2.2 by detailing the conditioning states, score head architecture, preference objective, and training setup.

sections.heading: Conditioning States.
sections.text: Following the main-text notation, we represent each candidate as q = ( 𝐈 ′ , 𝐚 ′ , 𝐬 ′ ) q=(\mathbf{I}^{\prime},\mathbf{a}^{\prime},\mathbf{s}^{\prime}) , where 𝐈 ′ \mathbf{I}^{\prime} is a real or generated video, 𝐚 ′ = ( a 1 ′ , … , a K ′ ) \mathbf{a}^{\prime}=(a_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,a_{K}^{\prime}) is the original or perturbed action chunk, and 𝐬 ′ = ( s 0 ′ , … , s K − 1 ′ ) \mathbf{s}^{\prime}=(s_{0}^{\prime},\ldots,s_{K-1}^{\prime}) is the corresponding state sequence. For both original and perturbed actions, we construct 𝐬 ′ \mathbf{s}^{\prime} by integrating the candidate’s own actions from the shared initial state s 0 s_{0} : s 0 ′ = s 0 , s t ′ = F ( s t − 1 ′ , a t ′ ) , t = 1 , … , K − 1 , s_{0}^{\prime}=s_{0},\qquad s_{t}^{\prime}=F(s_{t-1}^{\prime},a_{t}^{\prime}),\quad t=1,\ldots,K-1, (44) where F F updates the end-effector state using the relative action under the input conventions in Appendix D.1 . For action-mismatch pairs, the two candidates share the same real video and initial state, but each uses its own original or perturbed action chunk to construct its conditioning states. This keeps the states consistent with the actions and avoids conditioning the negative candidate on states obtained from the positive actions. For video-mismatch pairs, the candidates instead contain different generated videos but share the original action chunk and initial state, so they also share the integrated conditioning states. We use the same state construction during Flow-GRPO on Agi B \mathrm{Agi_{B}} , taking the initial state and action chunk from the AgiBotWorld recordings. The world model is conditioned on ( I 0 , 𝐚 ) (I_{0},\mathbf{a}) , and each generated video is scored with 𝐈 ′ = 𝐈 ^ \mathbf{I}^{\prime}=\hat{\mathbf{I}} , 𝐚 ′ = 𝐚 \mathbf{a}^{\prime}=\mathbf{a} , and the states 𝐬 ′ \mathbf{s}^{\prime} integrated from s 0 s_{0} and 𝐚 ′ \mathbf{a}^{\prime} . All candidates sampled under the same condition therefore share the actions and conditioning states. ACWM-RM combines these inputs with the candidate’s own visual history and evaluated frames, without requiring ground-truth future frames. In our offline experiments, actions are derived from differences between recorded end-effector states, so integrating them from s 0 s_{0} recovers the recorded trajectory. The conditioning states therefore contain trajectory information already encoded in the actions and initial state. Here, reference-free means that scoring requires no ground-truth future video or separately supplied future measured states.

sections.heading: Score Head Architecture.
sections.text: Here we specify the dimensions along the path from a pair of patch features to the reward score. The shared projection W proj ∈ ℝ d × D W_{\mathrm{proj}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times D} maps both branches from D = 1664 D=1664 down to d = 256 d=256 and is bias-free, so the five terms of Equation 3 , four of dimension d d and one scalar cosine similarity, concatenate into a comparison vector of dimension 4 ​ d + 1 = 1025 4d+1=1025 . Both MLPs of Equation 4 read this vector and share the architecture 1025 → 256 → 1 1025\rightarrow 256\rightarrow 1 with a GELU activation between the two affine layers, differing only in whether their output serves as a patch score or a patch weight. Together, W proj W_{\mathrm{proj}} and the two MLPs form h ψ h_{\psi} with 951,810 randomly initialized parameters. ACWM-RM has approximately 2.15B parameters in total, including the 1.84B frozen encoder, the 0.31B predictor, and the score head. During preference training, only the pretrained predictor and the randomly initialized score head are updated, giving approximately 0.31B trainable parameters. Gradients reach W proj W_{\mathrm{proj}} through both branches, while the encoded features are detached so that no gradient enters E E . We use the unbounded scalar output of Equation 5 directly as the reward, without a final sigmoid. The Bradley-Terry loss in Equation 45 applies the sigmoid to the score difference R + − R − R^{+}-R^{-} rather than to either candidate score individually.

sections.heading: D.3 Training Budget Accounting
sections.text: We report nominal training budgets in 13-frame clip draws, including repeated samples, based on corpus sizes before internal validation holdout. Each pretraining clip contributes one draw, while each preference pair contributes two candidate-clip draws. For each IDM, one draw likewise corresponds to a complete clip covering all 12 action transitions; predictions within a clip are not counted as separate draws. Pretraining samples one clip per episode per epoch, so 120 epochs over 34k episodes yield 120 × 34,000 = 4.08 ​ M 120\times 34{,}000=4.08\mathrm{M} clip draws. Preference training traverses 506.3k pairs for 3 epochs, yielding 3 × 506,300 = 1,518,900 3\times 506{,}300=1{,}518{,}900 pair draws, or 3,037,800 ≈ 3.04 ​ M 3{,}037{,}800\approx 3.04\mathrm{M} candidate-clip draws. sections.heading: Appendix E Training Setup for the Baseline IDMs
sections.text: We train four baseline IDMs on Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} , starting from the pretrained backbone checkpoints used in their official implementations. Specifically, EVA-IDM uses pretrained ResNet-50, GR00T-IDM uses pretrained SigLIP2-L/16, TAP-IDM uses pretrained Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and J-IDM uses pretrained VGGT. For each baseline, we follow its official implementation with the bimanual action-interface adaptations described below; the resulting architectures, observation-action interfaces, and hyperparameters are summarized in Tables 8 and 9 . TAP-IDM retains its original LM head and shared action-token vocabulary, configuring the FAST tokenizer to jointly decode 14-dimensional bimanual actions. J-IDM uses a 14-dimensional command space and a 28-channel per-pixel Jacobian head, jointly recovering both arms’ actions through ridge-regularized inversion. GR00T-IDM retains its 32-dimensional output with 20 valid components and padding masked during training; before reward computation, padding is discarded, and each arm’s 6D rotation is converted via quaternions to a 3D rotation-vector increment, yielding the 14-dimensional action layout in Eq. 6 . Its action horizon is set to 12, matching the 12 transitions in each 13-frame clip. For each IDM, we set a nominal budget of approximately 7.12M training clip draws, comparable to ACWM-RM’s combined budget (Appendix D.3 ). Each sampled clip contains 13 frames and 12 action transitions. We apply each IDM’s native observation window across the clip, with all 12 actions contributing to its training loss. After completing this budget, we select each IDM’s checkpoint by the lowest mean distance between its predicted actions and the ground-truth actions on the internal validation subset of Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} . sections.heading: Appendix F Prompt and Criteria for Evaluation
sections.text: You are a strict evaluator for a short generated robot-manipulation video. The input is a 13-frame clip; the first frame is the conditioning observation and the remaining 12 frames are generated. Given the task description, inspect every frame and score only the visible evidence. Evaluate: (i) object consistency , checking whether the manipulated object preserves its identity, shape, structure, color, material, and count; (ii) manipulator consistency , checking whether the robot, arms, hands, and grippers preserve their identity, geometry, connectivity, number of parts, and plausible articulation; and (iii) anomaly check , detecting floating or penetrating entities, teleportation, spontaneous appearance or disappearance, duplication, unsupported attachment, and false grasps. Assign each requested dimension a score from 1 (severe failure) to 5 (fully plausible and stable), using only information visible in the clip. Do not evaluate task completion or the final goal. Return a JSON object containing the scores and a brief evidence-based reason for each dimension. Table 11: Prompt used by Qwen3-VL to compute rewards during Flow-GRPO and by GPT-5.6 sol to evaluate the physical consistency of videos generated by DreamDojo after Flow-GRPO fine-tuning. When evaluating ACWM-generated videos for visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies, or using the VLM-based rewards to train the ACWM with Flow-GRPO, we use the evaluation prompt from RBench ( Deng et al., 2026 ) shown in Table 11 . The prompt produces three criteria: Object Consistency (OC), Manipulator Consistency (MC), and Anomaly Check (AC), each rated on an integer scale from 1 to 5. For the VLM-based rewards, we normalize each score to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and average the three normalized scores with equal weights to obtain the scalar reward used by Flow-GRPO: S VLM = 1 3 ​ ( OC − 1 4 + MC − 1 4 + AC − 1 4 ) . S_{\mathrm{VLM}}=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{\mathrm{OC}-1}{4}+\frac{\mathrm{MC}-1}{4}+\frac{\mathrm{AC}-1}{4}\right). The three criteria are defined as follows: • Object Consistency measures whether the target object preserves its identity and attributes throughout the video, including its shape, appearance, material, and count. • Manipulator Consistency measures the temporal stability of the robot embodiment, including its morphology, link or manipulator connectivity, joint articulation, and structural stability. • Anomaly Check measures physical and commonsense violations, such as floating or unsupported entities, interpenetration, spontaneous appearance or disappearance, duplication, non-contact attachment, and incorrect grasping.

sections.heading: Appendix G Flow-GRPO Optimization Details
sections.text: We fine-tune the policy using LoRA with rank 32 on 16 NVIDIA H800 GPUs. We optimize the LoRA parameters with AdamW at a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} for 120 outer training iterations. Each rollout uses 20 Flow-GRPO denoising steps and a diffusion noise level of 0.7 0.7 . Each sampled episode from Agi B \mathrm{Agi_{B}} (Table 13 ) supplies a shared input condition—the initial frame I 0 I_{0} and action chunk 𝐚 \mathbf{a} —for a group of G = 8 G=8 rollouts. In each outer iteration, we collect four rollout batches with a per-GPU sampling batch size of 8 episodes and group size G G , yielding 8 × 8 = 64 8\times 8=64 rollouts per batch and 256 rollouts per GPU per outer iteration. We then perform four inner PPO-style policy-optimization epochs on the collected data and accumulate gradients over 16 rollouts. The PPO-style ratio clipping range is 10 − 3 10^{-3} , the KL penalty coefficient is β = 0.004 \beta=0.004 , and gradients are clipped to a maximum norm of 1.0. We use seed 42 for policy optimization. ACWM-RM is frozen throughout policy optimization and uses the conditioning state sequence integrated from the initial state and each sampled action chunk. For evaluation on Agi C \mathrm{Agi_{C}} , we generate videos from each optimized ACWM using five video-generation seeds and report the mean and standard deviation across seeds for visual quality, action-following fidelity, and physical consistency.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.32222v1 [cs.CV] 23 Oct 2026 ACWM-RM: A Reference-Free Reward Model from Complementary Mismatch Preferences Shibo Hong Siyu Ren Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University Meituan FengJiao Chen Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University Meituan Zhongyuan Peng Wei Shi Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University Meituan Yixin Cao Abstract Reinforcement learning has gained attention for improving action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), as it enables reward-driven optimization of visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF) beyond flow-matching optimization. Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF. However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ. Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies. In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos. We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation. To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos. We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos. Evaluation on AVM-Eval reveals the limited reliability of IDMs on generated videos, while downstream RL experiments show that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in both criteria. 1 introduction Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2025 ) predict videos conditioned on robot actions, supporting embodied policy evaluation and optimization. For these applications, generated videos must preserve visual quality while faithfully reflecting the commanded actions. However, standard flow-matching training ( Lipman et al., 2022 ) does not explicitly optimize these criteria. This motivates reinforcement learning (RL) such as Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026a ) , which optimizes these criteria using rewards. The effectiveness of RL, however, depends on reward signals that reliably rank videos generated under the same conditioning input, assigning higher scores to those with better visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF). Existing reward signals fall into two main categories. First, full-reference rewards ( Wu et al., 2026b ) use metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS to compare generated videos with the corresponding ground-truth videos, providing VQ supervision but requiring reference videos and not directly assessing AF. Second, inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards ( Seo et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) assess AF without requiring reference videos by comparing actions inferred from generated videos with the input actions used to generate those videos, but do not directly assess VQ. Moreover, IDMs are typically trained on real-world videos, where motion and interactions obey physical laws, but are applied during RL to ACWM-generated videos that may contain visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies, such as robot-arm deformation and interpenetration. To quantify this issue, we generate 100 videos with each of four ACWMs under identical inputs. As shown in Figure , ACWM-generated videos exhibit more visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies than real-world videos. This gap raises the question of whether strong action-mismatch discrimination on real videos translates to reliable assessment of generated videos. In this work, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs. It evaluates how reliably IDMs assess AF on real videos using action-mismatch pairs and on generated videos using video-mismatch pairs. We then propose a reward model (ACWM-RM) for jointly assessing VQ and AF without ground-truth videos at reward computation time. To train ACWM-RM, we construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs of two types that provide complementary supervision: Action-mismatch pairs contrast original and perturbed actions for the same real video, providing AF supervision; Video-mismatch pairs contrast different generated videos under the same actions, providing VQ supervision while exposing the model to the generated-video distribution. For training strategy, we first pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on features extracted from real robot videos by a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) , establishing a dynamics representation for AF evaluation. We then jointly optimize the predictor and patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref, transferring the dynamics learned from real-world videos to AF assessment of generated videos. Our evaluation of four architecturally distinct IDMs on AVM-Eval shows that accurate AF assessment on real videos does not ensure reliable AF evaluation of generated videos. The best-performing IDM achieves 86.1% accuracy on action-mismatch pairs from real videos but only 70.0% on video-mismatch pairs from generated videos. To evaluate ACWM-RM’s downstream effectiveness as an RL reward, we fine-tune DreamDojo-2B with Flow-GRPO, comparing ACWM-RM against the best-performing IDM on AVM-Eval, a metric-based reward, and a VLM-based reward. On held-out tasks, ACWM-RM yields the best VQ and AF, while maintaining VLM-assessed physical consistency (PC) scores close to the original model before RL fine-tuning. Our main contributions: (1) We introduce AVM-Eval and show that, across four IDMs, accurate AF assessment on real videos does not ensure reliable AF evaluation of generated videos. (2) We develop AVM-Pref and ACWM-RM, combining dynamics pretraining with complementary mismatch preferences to assess both criteria without references during reward computation. (3) We demonstrate that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in VQ and AF when used for RL fine-tuning. 2 related work 2.1 Action-Conditioned World Models Action-conditioned world models generate videos conditioned on past observations and actions, simulating the resulting robot interactions to support policy evaluation and planning. To learn transferable dynamics, DreamDojo ( Gao et al., 2026 ) pretrains on human videos using continuous latent actions and adapts to target robots with robot data. To condition predictions on actions, iVideoGPT ( Wu et al., 2024 ) models observations and actions as token sequences with an autoregressive transformer, whereas IRASim ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) strengthens action-frame alignment through frame-level conditioning in a diffusion transformer. These predictive capabilities enable downstream applications: Genie Envisioner ( Liao et al., 2025 ) uses GE-Sim for action-conditioned simulation and closed-loop policy evaluation. Such applications require generated videos to preserve both VQ and AF, motivating our study of rewards that jointly assess these properties for ACWM post-training. 2.2 Reward Modeling for World Models Reliable reward signals are essential for effective RL, as they determine which properties of videos are optimized. For general video generation, VideoReward ( Liu et al., 2026b ) learns human preferences over visual quality and alignment. For embodied world models based on instructions, ReWorld ( Peng et al., 2026 ) and RoboAlign-R1 ( Wu et al., 2026a ) assess video quality and instruction alignment without evaluating correspondence with numerical actions. For action-conditioned world models, RLVR-World ( Wu et al., 2026b ) provides visual rewards through ground-truth video comparisons, while RLIR ( Ye et al., 2025 ) provides AF rewards by using IDM. Other dynamics-based rewards target different properties: EVA ( Wang et al., 2026 ) assesses action executability using IDM. However, reference-based rewards require ground truth, and IDMs that are accurate on real videos does not ensure reliable evaluation of generated videos or joint assessment of VQ and AF. 3 Preliminaries Given an initial frame I 0 I_{0} and an action chunk 𝐚 = ( a 1 , … , a K ) \mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{K}) , an ACWM p θ p_{\theta} predicts video 𝐈 ^ = ( I ^ 1 , … , I ^ K ) \hat{\mathbf{I}}=(\hat{I}_{1},\ldots,\hat{I}_{K}) by sampling 𝐈 ^ ∼ p θ ( ⋅ ∣ c ) \hat{\mathbf{I}}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c) , where c = ( I 0 , 𝐚 ) c=(I_{0},\mathbf{a}) . However, IDM-based rewards are applied to generated videos, whose distributions can differ from those of real-world videos. Generated videos may contain visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies, including robot-arm deformation and interpenetration, absent from real videos. To our knowledge, no existing benchmark compares the reliability of IDM-based AF assessment on real and generated videos. To address this gap, we construct AVM-Eval using a pairwise evaluation protocol ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) . AVM-Eval compares the reliability of AF assessment on real and ACWM-generated videos, using action-mismatch pairs and video-mismatch pairs , respectively. We next describe the source data preparation and benchmark construction. 4.1.1 Source data preparation We use AgiBotWorld ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , a large-scale bimanual robot dataset with real-world videos, as one source dataset, and partition its data by task into three subsets: Agi A \mathrm{Agi_{A}} , Agi B \mathrm{Agi_{B}} , and Agi C \mathrm{Agi_{C}} . Covering 36 tasks, Agi A \mathrm{Agi_{A}} is split at the episode level into 34.0k training episodes ( Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} ) for IDM, ACWM-RM predictor pretraining, and AVM-Pref construction, and 2.2k testing episodes ( Agi A test \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{test}} ) for constructing seen-task evaluation pairs in AVM-Eval. Using Agi ​ _ ​ B \mathrm{Agi\_B} , which contains 10.0k episodes across 30 tasks, we construct pairs for both unseen-task evaluation in AVM-Eval and RL fine-tuning. To evaluate RL-optimized ACWMs, we use Agi C \mathrm{Agi_{C}} , which contains 1.5k episodes across 10 tasks. Together, these two types constitute 67.2k pairs in AVM-Eval. Action-mismatch pairs (53.9k). To evaluate IDM-based AF assessment on real videos, we construct action-mismatch pairs. Each pair is represented as ( I 0 , 𝐚 + , 𝐚 − , 𝐈 ) (I_{0},\mathbf{a}^{+},\mathbf{a}^{-},\mathbf{I}) , where 𝐚 + \mathbf{a}^{+} is the action chunk recorded with 𝐈 \mathbf{I} and 𝐚 − \mathbf{a}^{-} is a perturbed counterpart. We generate 𝐚 − \mathbf{a}^{-} using two types of perturbations: Numerical Perturbations (N-P) and Semantic Perturbations (S-P). N-P probe sensitivity to low-level numerical errors in end-effector translation and rotation magnitudes or directions, gripper opening degree, and action ordering. S-P probe sensitivity to high-level semantic errors through position offsets during grasping or placement, incorrect gripper timing, and mid-motion drift or freeze. We also perturb action chunks from Gen \mathrm{Gen} , Robo D \mathrm{Robo_{D}} , and Robo T \mathrm{Robo_{T}} to assess IDM generalization across embodiments and scenes. Detailed perturbation procedures are provided in Appendix A . Video-mismatch pairs (13.3k). To evaluate AF on generated videos, we considered constructing action-mismatch pairs in the same way. However, ACWMs cannot guarantee that generated videos faithfully follow the action chunk, so a perturbed action chunk may be more consistent with the generated video than the original action chunk, reversing the intended preference label. We therefore construct video-mismatch pairs by fixing the action chunk and ranking generated videos using WorldArena’s nDTW ( Shang et al., 2026 ) for AF, with additional filtering to limit the influence of visual quality (Appendix B ). We use four ACWMs with varying AF performance: DreamDojo-2B (DD-2B), DreamDojo-14B (DD-14B) ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , GE-Sim-2B (GE-2B), and OSCAR-2B (OS-2B) ( Wu and Gao, 2026 ) . Under the same I 0 I_{0} and 𝐚 \mathbf{a} , each ACWM independently samples six 12-frame videos using the stochastic SDE sampler adopted by Flow-GRPO. Within each ACWM, we pair a higher-nDTW video 𝐈 ^ + \hat{\mathbf{I}}^{+} with a lower-nDTW video 𝐈 ^ − \hat{\mathbf{I}}^{-} to form an intra-model pair ( I 0 , 𝐚 , 𝐈 ^ + , 𝐈 ^ − ) (I_{0},\mathbf{a},\hat{\mathbf{I}}^{+},\hat{\mathbf{I}}^{-}) . We rank videos generated by any two ACWMs under the same input to construct cross-model pairs . 4.2 Reward Model for Action-Conditioned World Models Figure 1: Overview of (a,b) action-mismatch and video-mismatch pair construction for AVM-Eval and AVM-Pref, and (c) ACWM-RM reward computation without reference videos. Existing rewards provide only partial supervision, with metric-based rewards also requiring ground-truth videos. We therefore propose ACWM-RM, a reference-free reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF. We next describe the construction of its training dataset, termed AVM-Pref (Sec. 4.2.1 ), followed by the architecture and the two-stage training strategy (Sec. 4.2.2 ). 4.2.1 AVM-Pref Construction To train ACWM-RM with the Bradley-Terry loss, we construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) from Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} , comprising 506.3k action-mismatch and video-mismatch pairs that provide complementary supervision. Action-mismatch pairs (156.3k) : We use the same numerical and semantic action perturbations as AVM-Eval to provide AF supervision. Video-mismatch pairs (350k) : We follow AVM-Eval to generate videos from four ACWMs and construct intra-model and cross-model pairs, but use four visual quality metrics (global and local PSNR and LPIPS) instead of nDTW to provide VQ supervision. Since action-mismatch pairs already provide broader AF supervision than nDTW’s 2D trajectory alignment, including translation, rotation, and gripper opening, we use video-mismatch pairs for complementary VQ supervision. Although action-mismatch pairs use real videos and thus differ from the generated-video distribution, our empirical results show that combining both types improves AF assessment on generated videos. Finally, to reduce sampling bias, we aim for comparable pair counts across models and tasks for intra-model pairs and across model combinations and tasks for cross-model pairs. Appendix C details how the four metrics are used, while Appendix H provides AVM-Pref statistics. 4.2.2 Reward Model Architecture and Training Strategy ACWM-RM scores a candidate video conditioned on an action chunk and its associated state sequence, producing a scalar reward for VQ and AF. It consists of a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder E E , a bimanual action-conditioned predictor P ϕ P_{\phi} , and a patch-weighted score head h ψ h_{\psi} . Training proceeds in two stages: dynamics pretraining optimizes P ϕ P_{\phi} on real-world videos, while preference training jointly optimizes P ϕ P_{\phi} and h ψ h_{\psi} on AVM-Pref to adapt the learned dynamics for AF assessment. Dynamics pretraining. Following V-JEPA 2-AC ( Assran et al., 2025 ) , we pretrain P ϕ P_{\phi} with E E frozen. Unlike the original single-arm setting, our predictor takes bimanual actions. For bimanual inputs, we express actions and states in a coordinate system aligned with the head-camera axes, normalize them, project them to the predictor’s hidden dimension, and add a learnable identity embedding for each arm. On AVM-Eval, we compare ACWM-RM with four architecturally distinct IDMs: EVA-IDM ( EVA I \mathrm{EVA_{I}} ) ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , which uses a convolutional backbone; GR00T-IDM ( GRT I \mathrm{GRT_{I}} ) ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , which uses a diffusion-based model; TAP-IDM ( TAP I \mathrm{TAP_{I}} ) ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , a vision-language model equipped with an action expert; and J-IDM ( J I \mathrm{J_{I}} ) ( Li et al., 2026 ) , which recovers actions by inverting a predicted per-pixel Jacobian field. This evaluates how reliably IDMs with different architectures transfer from real-video training to generated-video evaluation. For Flow-GRPO training of ACWMs, we compare ACWM-RM with IDM-based, metric-based, and VLM-based rewards. The IDM-based baseline uses the best-performing IDM on AVM-Eval. We further explore whether VLM-as-a-Judge ( Hong et al., 2025 ) can provide effective rewards for ACWM optimization. Specifically, we use Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct to score videos using embodiment-specific prompts and criteria from RBench. Prompts and criteria definitions are provided in the Appendix F . Visual quality. ACWM-RM achieves the best results across all five VQ metrics in Table 5 , outperforming the full-reference metric-based reward. Unlike this baseline, ACWM-RM requires no ground-truth videos for reward computation during RL. Although its training preferences are derived from PSNR and LPIPS, the gains extend to SSIM, MSE, and FVD, which are not used for preference supervision. In contrast, the IDM-based reward degrades all five metrics relative to Origin, suggesting that optimizing IDM-based AF alone is insufficient to preserve visual quality. Action-following fidelity. Table 4 shows that ACWM-RM is the only evaluated reward that improves nDTW over Origin, from 14.84 to 16.41. The VLM-based and metric-based rewards yield no improvement, while the IDM-based reward reduces nDTW to 13.21 despite explicitly measuring consistency between inferred and conditioning actions. Together with the AVM-Eval findings, these results suggest that strong action-mismatch discrimination on real videos does not necessarily translate into an effective RL reward for improving action-following fidelity. Physical consistency. Although ACWM-RM does not explicitly reward physical consistency, the model optimized with it achieves scores comparable to Origin across all three criteria in Table 5 . By contrast, the VLM-based reward yields a lower overall physical-consistency score than Origin (3.86 vs. 4.00), despite directly targeting these criteria. One possible explanation is disagreement between the VLMs used for reward computation and evaluation: optimizing scores assigned by the reward VLM may not improve physical consistency as judged by the evaluation VLM. 5.4 Ablation Study Score head architecture. We examine whether real-video dynamics pretraining and joint preference training improve AF assessment. We construct two variants using the same score head and AVM-Pref: Fresh Predictor jointly trains a randomly initialized predictor and the head, while Frozen Predictor trains only the head with the pretrained predictor fixed. Compared with Fresh Predictor, Ours improves action-mismatch accuracy from 85.0 to 91.6 and video-mismatch accuracy from 62.0 to 88.6 (Table 6 ). These gains support the value of learning dynamics before preference training. Compared with Frozen Predictor, Ours improves video-mismatch accuracy from 79.0 to 88.6 under the same preference supervision, showing that adapting the pretrained predictor during preference training further benefits AF assessment on generated videos. Comparison with an inverse-dynamics architecture. To assess whether ACWM-RM’s advantage can be explained solely by exposure to preference data, we construct JEPA-IDM with the same frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and predictor backbone, but use action prediction instead of visual-feature prediction. Following the IDM reward formulation, JEPA-IDM uses action-prediction errors as rewards and undergoes action-prediction pretraining on real videos from Agi A train \mathrm{Agi_{A}^{train}} , followed by preference training on AVM-Pref. Implementation details are provided in Appendix I . As shown in Table 6 , ACWM-RM outperforms JEPA-IDM by 3.1 points on action-mismatch pairs (91.6 vs. 88.5) and 14.9 points on video-mismatch pairs (88.6 vs. 73.7). The larger gap on generated videos supports the benefit of ACWM-RM’s feature prediction and scoring design, even when JEPA-IDM has the same backbone and training data and follows the same two-stage training paradigm. 6 Conclusion, Limitations, and Future Work Through AVM-Eval, we showed that strong action-mismatch discrimination on real videos does not ensure reliable AF assessment of generated videos. To address this limitation while also assessing VQ, we introduced ACWM-RM, a reward model requiring no ground-truth videos for reward computation. ACWM-RM outperforms IDMs on generated-video AF and, when used to fine-tune DreamDojo-2B, yields better VQ and AF than alternative reward signals. Limitations and future work. ACWM-RM is trained to assess VQ and AF, but does not explicitly supervise physical consistency (PC). Although RL fine-tuning with ACWM-RM maintains PC scores close to those of the pre-RL model, the reward does not directly target physical violations such as interpenetration. Moreover, downstream RL improvements have so far been demonstrated only for DreamDojo-2B on AgiBotWorld.
